source_text: Exercui hunc locum in secundo prioris operis libello, atque ostendi, prius in homine concupiscentiam carnis quae speciem irritat saporis et oculorum fuisse, quam culpam.
pass_a_gloss: I worked this place in the second little book of the earlier work, and I showed that the desire of the flesh which stirs the appearance of taste and of the eyes was in the human being before fault.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS opus; Blaise God's works vs devil's

pass_b_english: I treated this passage in the second book of my earlier work and showed that the desire of the flesh, which stirs the appeal of taste and sight, existed in the human being before guilt did (compare Genesis 3:6).

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
